t: Longer Contiguous Segments of Ones than Zeros — One-Pass Run Tracking
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Scan the binary string s and compare two quantities: the length of the longest consecutive block of 1s and the longest consecutive block of 0s. Return true only when the 1s block is strictly longer; if a character never appears, its longest segment counts as 0.

**Walking through Example 1:** s = 1101 splits into runs 11, 0, 1. Longest run of 1s is 2 (from 11), longest run of 0s is 1, so 2 > 1 returns true.

**Example 2:** s = 111000 has runs 111 then 000 — both maximal segments are exactly 3, and strict inequality fails, so the answer is false.

**Example 3:** s = 110100010 contains 11 (length 2) as the best 1-run while 000 reaches 3, so it is false.

**What the constraints imply:** with n up to 100 any approach works, but the natural solution is a single O(n) pass tracking the current streak, or even simpler, splitting the string into runs per character.
k: Only maximal runs matter: extend the current streak while characters match and reset it to 1 on every change.
The comparison must be strict — equal longest runs return false.
A missing character contributes a best-run of 0, which falls out automatically if counters start at zero.

a.n: Approach 1: Single Pass with Streak Counters
a.i: Walk the string once holding the current run length and the previous character. When the character repeats, grow the streak; when it flips, reset it to 1. After each step, update that character's best-seen run. One boolean comparison at the end finishes the job.
s: Track cur (current run length), prev (previous character), and best runs bestOne / bestZero, all starting appropriately at zero.
For each ch: cur = cur + 1 if ch == prev else 1.
Update the best counter for ch with max(best, cur); set prev = ch.
a.t: O(n) — each character is examined once with constant work.
a.sp: O(1) — three integers and one character.

a.n: Approach 2: Split into Runs per Character
a.i: Splitting s on the separator 0 yields exactly the maximal blocks of 1s (empty strings between adjacent separators contribute length 0 and are harmless); splitting on 1 yields the 0-blocks. The answer compares the maximum piece lengths of both splittings. This expresses the idea declaratively — no manual streak bookkeeping — at the cost of building substrings.
s: Compute ones = max length among pieces of s.split('0').
Compute zeros = max length among pieces of s.split('1').
a.t: O(n) — each split touches every character a constant number of times.
a.sp: O(n) — the split materializes substring pieces before reducing them.

w: Approach 1 is the interview default — say single pass, constant space, done. Pitfalls: using >= instead of strict > (Example 2 exists to catch exactly that), resetting the streak on every iteration instead of only on character change, and forgetting the missing-character rule — though initializing best counters to 0 handles strings like 111 or 0 for free. Edge cases worth mentioning: single-character strings return true when the character is 1 and false when it is 0. Follow-ups: report the position of the longest run, generalize to k distinct symbols, or handle streams where the string cannot fit in memory (the streaming-friendly Approach 1 still works).
